newsitem.title: USA: U.S. blames Milosevic for Belgrade violence.
newsitem.headline: U.S. blames Milosevic for Belgrade violence.

text.p: The United States said on Tuesday it held Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic responsible for street battles in Belgrade between government supporters and opponents protesting the annulment of local elections the oppostion appeared to have won.

"The U.S. holds the Serbian government and its president, Slobodan Milosevic, responsible for the violent actions of the demonstrators," acting Secretary of State Strobe Talbott said in a statement. "The U.S. government condemns violence by pro-Milosevic demonstrators in Belgrade."
Talbott said the top U.S. diplomat in Belgrade, Richard Miles, had met Serbian Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic on Tuesday to urge the government to avoid further violence.

"We have given a similar message to the opposition," he said after a day of street of battles in which a man was shot in the head. "We call on all sides to exercise maximum restraint and avoid further confrontation."

About 40,000 Milosevic supporters, a fraction of those expected, turned out for a pro-government rally, a blow to Milosevic's attempts to quell 35 days of protests by opposition Zajedno (Together) parties who accused him of election fraud after he voided their victories in Nov. 17 municipal elections.
Talbott placed the responsiblity for the flareup squarely on the government, which had called on its supporters to stage a huge rally in downtown Belgrade, site of the opposition protests.

"Rather than making a goodwill effort to resolve the political crisis caused by the annulment of oppostion victories in the Nov. 17 elections, the Serbian authorities have flagrantly and provocatively chosen to heighten tensions by bringing thousands of people into Belgrade to confront the peaceful demonstrations by the opposition," he said.

The United States reiterated its call on Serbia's government to respect the results of the election, open a dialogue with the democratic opposition and "refrain from any further actions to incite unrest."

"We have warned the Serbian government that violence against the protesters will have serious consequences and will inevitably lead to Serbia's further isolation from the international community," Talbott said.

The decision by Milosevic backers to hold their rally outside Zajedno's headquarters at the same time as the daily opposition demonstration plunged the city centre into chaos. Rival groups fought running battles with sticks and iron bars and a gunman who fired from a group of Milosevic supporters seriously injured a young man in the head.

Independent media said seven people were treated for knife wounds and several police were reported hurt. Police separated the demonstrators but took an hour to push Zajedno supporters away from the stand erected for Milosevic's speech.

The violence was the first since Zajedno began its protests against Milosevic's suppression of local election victories. Some analysts predicted the authorities would use it as an excuse to ban future demonstrations or to declare a state of emergency.
Milosevic, under threat of Western reprisals, had not previously used his police against the demonstrations, the biggest since 1992 when he used tanks to quell unrest.
